body_markdown:
It was a simple promise, one of a body-on-frame pickup with modesty as its selling point. The dimensions are tidy. There’s a mandatory four-cylinder engine, with no cost or maintenance concerns from the addition of forced induction or direct injection. The engine is teamed up with a manual or automatic gearbox, and the body is designed by the legendary[Frank Stephenson](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/how-frank-stephenson-turned-the-ferrari-360-into-the-f430/) , whose name has graced the designs of Ferraris, McLarens, and the new Mini. Now we have more information, a handful of digital renderings, and a trio of affordable price tags for what could be the most perfect truck in decades.


Stephenson and his[design company](https://www.frankstephenson.com/) were given the task of designing a simple and cost-effective vehicle with three unique body styles atop the same 119.6-inch wheelbase, sharing DNA upstream of REO’s corporate[B-pillar](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-a-glossary-of-automotive-design-terms/#:~:text=B%2Dpillar%3A%20The%20second%20pillar%20of%20a%20roof%2C%20when%20moving%20backward%20from%20a%20vehicle%E2%80%99s%20nose%2C%20after%20the%20A%2Dpillar.) and corporate front end. That fascia has a bit of a Jeep Cherokee (XJ) look, with a large but understated grille set within a subtly chiseled nose. There are stacked headlights akin to a squarebody Chevy truck, or the XJ Cherokee Wagoneer, if you want to get picky. The bumper looks like an aftermarket steel affair from Ranch Hand, though it and items like the door panels, headliner, and trim are supposedly removable in under five minutes with common tools.


REO Trucks


We discussed REO and its CEO[in a previous story](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-story-of-the-small-truck-past-present-and-future/#:~:text=Dredging%20up%2C%20and,I%20find%20conceivable.) this summer, before we sampled a[Slate EV](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/i-drove-267-miles-to-not-drive-a-slate-truck/) truck and heard about[Ford’s upcoming Fathom](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/getting-to-the-bottom-of-fords-28350-fathom/) . But we now have more details on REO’s three products, and this latest news suggests all derivations remain true to what made them set social media on fire this summer: open-source repair information, no software locks, no subscriptions, no traditional car dealerships, and readily available factory and aftermarket parts.


While no interior or production details are provided, the exterior insights on each REO vehicle are certainly appealing. And worth a closer look:


## Runabout T4X – $21,500 (estimated)


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


The[cheapest REO is a regular cab work truck](https://reotrucks.com/runabout/t4x) with two seats, a separate 6.5-foot bed, and a massive B-pillar. This is significantly different from a Slate EV, which utilizes a unitized body and a 5-foot bed that theoretically cannot handle the same payload weight. A separate bed is less likely to damage the entire truck under load, as the renderings suggest a painted metal body over the Slate’s plastic construction. The bed also features a dropside design, with a flat floor, much like those rigs you rent from Home Depot or what’s commonplace in the Japanese Kei truck market.


An enclosed storage nook rests between the cab and the rear axle, suggesting this rig can be ready for just about any activity a compact truck can handle. REO estimates a base price of $21,500, which is thousands less than the Slate EV. REO is targeting a 5000lb tow rating, 22-25 miles per gallon (combined city and highway), a 500-600-mile range, and a lofty powertrain life of 500,000 miles.


There is a Ransom edition (named after[Ransom Olds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ransom_E._Olds) , *natch* ) that’s akin to a Z71 Chevy, a TRD Toyota, or an FX4 Ford. A taller ride height and more aggressive shocks are expected, and the Ransom has better approach (42.5° / 48.3°), departure (17.4° / 20.5°), and breakover (16.3° / 21.2°) angles than a stock REO.


## Runabout T4C – $25,000 (estimated)


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


This[four-door Runabout T4C](https://reotrucks.com/runabout/t4c) has a significantly different body than the T4X, suggesting the addition of two more doors turns this truck into a single-body affair like the 2001-2013 Chevrolet Avalanche. This configuration has five seats with two rows, and an overall length shorter by about an inch (195.6 inches). REO suggests this rig will tow the same 5000 lbs, but payload capacities are still unknown.


All REOs share the same wheelbase, and these renderings suggest this makes the rear doors as tight around the legs as the aforementioned XJ Jeep Cherokee. The bed no longer drops down, and it’s deep enough to mandate bumps for the wheel arches. The Runabout T4C is estimated to have a $25,000 base price.


## Runabout S4C – $28,500 (estimated)


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


REO Trucks


And if the previous model was a Chevy Avalanche, the[Runabout S4C](https://reotrucks.com/runabout/s4c) is a Chevy Tahoe incarnate. This REO seats six passengers via the addition of a jump seat. The latter throne is likely similar to the cramped affairs of extended-cab Rangers and S-10s of the past, as this fully enclosed SUV has a shorter overall length (182.7 inches) than the T4C. There is a lockable storage compartment opposite the jump seat, and the significantly larger interior is likely the primary reason why this is the most expensive REO at $28,500.


With these prices and REO’s proud proclamation of internal combustion motivation, this Texas startup appears to offer a significant value proposition. In theory, REO is courting everyone from the traditional side-by-side powersports customer to those looking at Kei trucks, be it older examples or the new[Scion Kei-01](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/a-u-s-market-kei-truck-with-a-scion-badge-its-happening/) . While pricing for the Scion isn’t known as of yet, odds are Toyota’s penchant for premium pricing will likely put it ahead of the REO.


The other genre of players in this space is electrified, and currently occupied by the Slate EV truck and the upcoming Ford Fathom. Both EVs are likely to be more car-like, as the Slate I sampled was downright El Camino-like in body construction, and Ford’s electric trucklet is the first offering of a chassis intended for a whole class of affordable vehicles. But Slate is far ahead of the game, with prototypes and a promise to begin deliveries in Q1 2027. The theoretical Ford isn’t far behind, and it’s unlikely to disappear after a[2 billion dollar Kentucky commitment](https://www.fromtheroad.ford.com/us/en/articles/2025/inside-new-ford-universal-ev-production-system) to a Universal EV platform.


There’s a lot to like about REO and their trio of trucks. But it’s worth tempering your excitement for at least a moment: they are currently a private company with no listed investors, unlike all the Amazon alumni-backed hoopla around Slate. That name recognition lent Slate an air of financial stability that REO currently lacks; however, REO says they’ve taken over 40,000 paid reservations for their product. At $25 (refundable, too), that potentially put a million bucks into their coffers. If true, that could provide adequate incentive for well-heeled private investors to also cut them a check. REO has been pretty silent about that matter, but[Expedition Portal](https://expeditionportal.com/texas-based-reo-trucks-plans-21500-gas-pickup/) suggests they have backing from the likes of “automotive suppliers, logistics industry executives, and several Midwest manufacturing firms.”


Whether or not REO is a going concern is anyone’s guess at the moment, but there’s no doubt they are using all the right words. And they certainly got Frank Stephenson to whip them up an honest-looking little truck for the job.
